694.title: Your own feast days
694.hook: many Catholics keep their baptism day and their saint's name day
694.howItsDone: In many Catholic countries people celebrate the feast of the saint whose name they bear, with greetings, cake or a small gift, and some families also mark each child's baptism anniversary, sometimes by lighting the baptismal candle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day, Sunday as the first day of a new creation. Your line was a little easter. What did you plan to set down this Sunday? Day six hundred ninety-four.

In a Polish office in late July, someone walks in with a box of pastries, and the whole floor sings to Anna. It isn't her birthday. Nobody there knows her birthday. It's the feast of Saint Anne, and so it's her imieniny, her name day. Orthodox neighbors in Greece keep it too: the same thing happens to every Giorgos on Saint George's day, and the phone doesn't stop ringing. The calendar of saints we've been walking through all year isn't only the Church's calendar. In some places, it's personal.
screen: `PASTRIES FOR ANNA.` → `NOT HER BIRTHDAY.` → `A CALENDAR THAT GETS PERSONAL.`

segments.voice: A name day is the feast of the saint whose name you carry. For centuries Catholic children were usually baptized with a saint's name, and that saint became their patron: a friend in heaven, an example, someone to ask for prayers. Church law still asks parents, godparents and the pastor not to give a name foreign to Christian sense, though it doesn't require a saint's name. The Catechism puts it this way, in paraphrase: in baptism the Lord's name sanctifies a person, and a Christian receives his or her own name in the Church. Behind that is an old line from Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims, God says to his people: "I have redeemed thee, and called thee by thy name: thou art mine." In much of Catholic Europe and Latin America, the name day was once a bigger party than the birthday. Italians call it the onomastico; Poles, imieniny. Then there's a second feast many Catholics keep: the day of their baptism. Pope Francis often asked people in his audiences whether they knew the date of their own baptism, and suggested they find out and celebrate it like a birthday, because for Catholics that day is a kind of birth. Some families light the baptismal candle again each year. And if your name isn't a saint's name? Many people take a patron at confirmation. Others look for a saint born in their town, or sharing their job, or their birthday. The point isn't the name itself. It's that the great calendar of the Church has a door in it with your name on the front.
screen: `A SAINT'S NAME AT BAPTISM.` · `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.` · `ONOMASTICO, IMIENINY.` · `YOUR BAPTISM DAY, LIKE A BIRTHDAY.` · then, large: `THOU ART MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your name saint. Settle, and breathe. Say your own first name, slowly, in your head. Is there a saint who carries it, or something close? If you know, picture that person: where they lived, what they're remembered for. If you don't know, choose a question to look up after the bell: whose name do I carry, and when is their day? If you're baptized, add one more: what was the date? If you pray, you can ask your saint to pray for you. The bell holds the time.
Name day. The feast of the saint whose name you were given, kept in many Catholic countries like a second birthday. Today's word.
Your line: your own feast. Today, look up your name saint's day or your baptism date, and put it in your calendar for next time. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: The three-year cycle
695.hook: Sundays read Matthew, then Mark, then Luke, with John in Lent and Easter
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book is a person
695.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass Catholics hear an Old Testament reading, a Psalm, a reading from the letters and a Gospel set by the lectionary's three-year cycle; many missals and apps show the year's letter and the readings for each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name day, the feast of the saint whose name you carry. Your line was your own feast. Did you find your saint, or your baptism date? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Go to Mass in Chicago this Sunday, then fly to Manila and go again next week, and you'll notice something. The same Gospel passages, in the same order, in a different language. A Catholic who goes every Sunday for three years will hear a large share of all four Gospels read aloud, without ever choosing a passage. And many Sunday missals print a single capital letter that tells you where you are. Today, the letter.
screen: `CHICAGO, THEN MANILA.` → `THE SAME GOSPEL, ANOTHER LANGUAGE.` → `ONE CAPITAL LETTER.`

segments.voice: The Second Vatican Council asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up more lavishly, so that people would hear a fuller share of scripture over a set number of years. The answer was a new lectionary, the book of readings, issued in 1969. Before it, most Sundays repeated the same readings every year. The new one spread the Sunday Gospels over three years. Year A reads Matthew. Year B reads Mark. Year C reads Luke. John has no year of his own, because he gets the great seasons: much of Lent and Easter in every year, and in Year B, which is short because Mark is short, five Sundays of summer go to John chapter six, the bread of life. Each Sunday also has an Old Testament reading chosen to echo the Gospel, a Psalm, and a reading from the letters. The weekdays run on a separate two-year cycle for the first reading. The cycle turns over on the First Sunday of Advent, not on New Year's Day. Here's the trick for finding the letter: take the calendar year in which the Church's year ends and divide it by three. No remainder means Year C. A remainder of one means A. A remainder of two means B. So the year that ends in November 2026 is Year A, Matthew, and Advent 2026 begins Year B. It reached beyond Catholic churches too: many Protestant churches use the Revised Common Lectionary, which grew out of it, so on a given Sunday neighbors down the street may hear the same Gospel. And this is the last day of the year of feasts. Tomorrow, the close of year two.
screen: `A NEW LECTIONARY, 1969.` · `A IS MATTHEW, B IS MARK, C IS LUKE.` · `JOHN IN LENT, EASTER AND YEAR B'S SUMMER.` · `DIVIDE THE YEAR BY THREE.` · then, large: `A, B, C.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find this year's letter. Settle, and breathe. Think of the year the Church's current year ends in, and divide it by three in your head. Take your time. When you've got the letter, think of the Gospel that goes with it, and one story from that Gospel you remember from these two years: a parable, a healing, a meal. Hold that one scene for the rest of the sit, as if you were hearing it read aloud on Sunday. The bell holds the time.
The three-year cycle. The Sunday readings at Mass, Matthew in Year A, Mark in Year B, Luke in Year C, with John woven through the great seasons. Today's word.
Your line: a, b, c. Today, look up this Sunday's Gospel, find its letter, and read it before Sunday comes. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the book is a person
696.hook: a whole Bible in order, and the Church's year; Catholics say every page points to Christ
696.tomorrow: Year three opens: the story after Acts
696.howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole sweep of scripture read at Mass through the Church's year, and the Church encourages personal reading too, often slowly, as in lectio divina, with the Gospels at the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three-year cycle: Matthew, Mark and Luke in turn, with John in the great seasons. Your line was a, b, c. Did you find this year's letter? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

On the evening of the first Easter, two disciples are walking home to a village called Emmaus, seven miles of dust and disappointment. A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about. They tell him everything: the hopes, the cross, the strange report of an empty tomb. And the stranger, instead of comforting them, starts at the beginning of their own scriptures and walks them through it, page after page, all the way home. Later they'll say their hearts were burning. That walk is where year two ends.
screen: `THE ROAD TO EMMAUS.` → `A STRANGER WALKS BESIDE THEM.` → `PAGE AFTER PAGE, ALL THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them in all the scriptures, the things that were concerning him." That's the Catholic way of reading the whole Bible, and it's the road you've walked this year. First, the beginning: Genesis, a garden, a flood, Abraham's tent, Joseph forgiving his brothers. Then out of Egypt: the sea, the mountain, the law. Then the kings, the prophets, the wisdom books, and the seven books Catholic Bibles keep, from Tobit to the Maccabees. Second, the Gospels: Luke's mercy, then John's signs and his Word made flesh. Third, the Church on the move: Acts, Paul's letters from Romans to Philemon, Hebrews and James, Peter, John and Jude, and the Apocalypse with its new heaven and new earth. Fourth, the year of feasts: Advent to Christ the King, and this last week, Friday, Saturday, Sunday and your own name. Saint Augustine put the Catholic reading in a famous pair: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, said it more sharply: not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ. That's what the carry means. For Catholics, the Bible isn't finally a book of rules or a book of history, though it holds both. It's a long way of meeting someone. And on that road, the disciples knew the stranger at last when he broke the bread. Tomorrow, year three: the story after Acts, the long history of the Church.
screen: `FROM GENESIS TO THE SEVEN BOOKS.` · `LUKE, THEN JOHN.` · `ACTS, THE LETTERS, THE APOCALYPSE.` · `THE YEAR OF FEASTS.` · then, large: `THE THINGS THAT WERE CONCERNING HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one book to keep reading. Settle, and breathe. Let this year's books pass by, not in order, just as they come: a garden, a burning bush, a psalm, a prodigal son walking home, a Samaritan woman at a well, a shipwreck, a letter, a city coming down from heaven. Notice which one tugs at you. Don't argue with it. That's the book you keep. Picture yourself opening it again next week, a few verses at a time. If you pray, you can ask to recognize him in it. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. The whole Bible in order and the Church's year of feasts, read the way Catholics read it: every page pointing to Christ. Today's word.
Your line: the book is a person. Today, open the book you chose and read one page, slowly, the way you'd listen to someone you're getting to know. Day six hundred ninety-six.
